name: Absorbance to Transmittance Converter
seoDesc: Absorbance and transmittance are two ways of writing the same measurement, related by a base-ten logarithm. Free absorbance to transmittance converter calcula
summary:
Absorbance and transmittance are two ways of writing the same measurement, related by a base-ten logarithm. It returns transmittance, transmittance, concentration from Beer–Lambert and fraction of light lost, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This converter goes both ways, adds percent transmission and the concentration the reading implies at a chosen extinction coefficient. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Absorbance to Transmittance Converter
sections.html:
A = −log₁₀(T) = 2 − log₁₀(%T); T = 10^(−A); A = ε·c·l

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Aabsorbance (optical density)—
Ttransmittance as a fraction—
εextinction coefficientper mg/mL
lpath lengthcm

sections.title: How do I use the Absorbance to Transmittance Converter?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: absorbance of 0.5, extinction coefficient of 1 per mg/mL, path length of 1 cm.

Substituting them into the formula gives transmittance of 0.3162, transmittance of 31.62%, concentration from beer–lambert of 0.5 mg/mL, fraction of light lost of 68.38%.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
0 – 0.1Very dilutepoor signal-to-noise on most instruments
0.1 – 1.0Reliablethe linear window of a spectrophotometer
1.0 – 1.5Highstray light starts to bend the curve
above 2.0Unreliabledilute the sample and multiply the result

  • An absorbance of 1.0 means 10% of the light got through; 2.0 means 1%. This is why a doubling of absorbance corresponds to ten times less light, not half.

  • Instruments quote linear range up to about 1.0–1.5 A, above which stray light makes the reading saturate. Always dilute and multiply.

  • Transmittance is sometimes quoted as a percentage in older methods; 50% T is 0.301 A, not 0.5 A.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Treating absorbance as linear in transmittance: doubling A does not halve T.
  • Using a cuvette with the wrong path length and forgetting to scale c.
  • Forgetting the blank, which shifts every reading by its own absorbance.

faq.q: What is an absorbance of 2 in transmittance?
Why does my reading stop increasing when I add more sample?
faq.a: The instrument has reached the top of its linear range and stray light now dominates.

faq.q: What does the Absorbance to Transmittance Converter actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns transmittance, transmittance, concentration from Beer–Lambert and fraction of light lost. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
